newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW - No concern over Japan regional banks - MOF.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - No concern over Japan regional banks - MOF.

text.p: Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) does not think there will be more failures of Japanese regional banks if current economic conditions prevail, a senior MOF official told Reuters on Thursday.

Sei Nakai, deputy director-general of MOF's Banking Bureau, said in an interview that while the ministry was well aware of market rumours that there were more debt-ridden regional banks like the failed Hanwa Bank Ltd, such concerns were not warranted.
"There are no problems with the business of regional banks, including second-tier regional banks about which there have been rumours," Nakai said.

Auditors for Hanwa Bank had called on it to write off massive problem loans in the first half of fiscal 1996/97 to September 30, and this had led to the bank having an excess of liabilities over assets.
After learning of Hanwa's financial situation, MOF decided to step in to close the bank, Nakai said.
Half-year audits at other banks had shown no other serious financial problems like Hanwa's, he said.
While banks' future financial health would be influenced by the economic conditions and land prices, there were no reasons to worry if the current economic conditions continued, he said.
Even if interest rates rose and unrealised profits on shareholdings fell to some extent from current levels, there would be no problem for their business, he said.
"Banks are also trying hard to restructure themselves and to dispose of problem loans," he added.

Earlier on Thursday, the Finance Ministry announced that it had suspended all business at Hanwa Bank except for deposit withdrawals because the bank could not recover its bad loans and was unable to operate as a going concern.
Hanwa is a second-tier regional bank based in western Japan.
Nakai said its collapse was a domestic, regional issue as the 500 billion yen in deposits at Hanwa accounted for only 0.08 percent of the total at Japanese financial institutions.
He also said that Hanwa does not have branches overseas.

Asked about funds available over the next five years for the Deposit Insurance Corp of Japan to cover the Hanwa failure and any future failures of financial institutions, Nakai said the funds would be sufficient.

Nakai said funds available from the Deposit Insurance Corp would total 2.7 trillion yen over the next five years and Japanese authorities would review the level of the insurance premium after three years.
While the ministry saw the size of the funds as sufficient to cover any future failures, the review was a precaution, he said.

Nakai said that private sector banks would be able to cope with problem loans held by non-bank financial institutions -- those which do not take deposits and depend mainly on bank loans for their lending business.
"Many of the loans to troubled non-banks have been counted as problem loans. Banks have set aside loan loss provisions (on those loans)," he said.
